lesson.title: Cell Drinking: Pinocytosis and the Nonstop Sipping of Extracellular Fluid
lesson.summary: Pinocytosis is the continuous, fluid-phase form of endocytosis in which a cell takes in small droplets of extracellular fluid along with whatever solutes happen to be dissolved in it.
lesson.body:
Where phagocytosis is a dramatic, targeted response to a specific large particle, pinocytosis, whose name comes from Greek roots meaning cell drinking, is a quieter and more continuous process. Instead of extending pseudopodia around a discrete object, the plasma membrane simply invaginates inward at many points across its surface, forming small pockets that pinch off into tiny vesicles carrying droplets of the surrounding extracellular fluid, along with whatever ions, small proteins, and other dissolved solutes happen to be present in that fluid at that moment.

Because pinocytosis does not require recognizing and binding a specific large target, it is often described as fluid-phase endocytosis, and many types of cells carry it out more or less constantly as part of normal membrane turnover, sampling their surroundings in small, continuous sips rather than large, occasional gulps. This does not mean pinocytosis is entirely nonspecific, however. Many cells also carry out a receptor-mediated version of the same basic process, in which membrane receptors bind particular dissolved molecules, such as specific proteins present at low concentration in extracellular fluid, and concentrate them at sites where small vesicles are about to form, giving the cell a way to take up scarce solutes efficiently even through a mechanism that is otherwise fairly indiscriminate.

The vesicles produced by pinocytosis are consistently much smaller than a typical phagosome, since they are forming around a droplet of fluid rather than folding around a bulky particle, and their formation generally requires less localized cytoskeletal remodeling than the pseudopodia extension seen in phagocytosis. Once formed, pinocytotic vesicles follow a route similar to other endocytic vesicles, often fusing with endosomes and eventually lysosomes so that any useful solutes can be extracted and the membrane components recycled back toward the cell surface.

Pinocytosis plays an especially important role in tissues that need to reclaim dissolved material from a fluid stream passing across their surface. Cells lining the small intestine use pinocytosis to help take up certain nutrients and small proteins from digested food, supplementing the more selective, carrier-based absorption mechanisms discussed earlier. In the kidney, cells lining sections of the tubules use pinocytosis to reclaim small proteins that have passed through the filtration barrier of the glomerulus, preventing the loss of proteins that would otherwise be excreted uselessly in urine.

Together, phagocytosis and pinocytosis show how the single underlying strategy behind endocytosis, wrapping extracellular material in a pinched-off piece of the plasma membrane, can be tuned to handle very different jobs. Phagocytosis is built for large, discrete particles and depends heavily on receptor recognition and actin-driven engulfment, while pinocytosis is built for continuous, low-volume sampling of fluid and its dissolved contents, running almost constantly in many cell types as a routine part of maintaining the cell's relationship with its environment.
